Off The Mark: On Aaron Sorkin's "The Social Reckoning"
Kyle Turner reviews the worst journalism movie of the year  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

Off The Mark: On Aaron Sorkin's "The Social Reckoning"
Kyle Turner reviews the worst journalism movie of the year
Journalism and AI:
Addressing Fears, Anxieties, and Concerns
Wednesday, October 28, 2026
10:00 AM PT / 1:00 PM ET
Sign up
Off the Mark: On Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning “
by
Kyle Turner
Share on
X
, Share on
Bluesky
Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) and Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) in Columbia Pictures’ THE SOCIAL RECKONING.
Courtesy of Sony Pictures
Everyone loves a journalism movie. We love Dustin Hoffman and Robert Redford on the trail of Watergate in
All the President’s Men
; we adore Holly Hunter and William Hurt figuring out what honest reporting looks like in
Broadcast News
; we are enamored of Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell bickering out of one side of their mouths in
His Girl Friday
. Movies set in the Fourth Estate feel nearly as institutional as the offices they’re set in. Typically, the thrill of a journalism movie is in witnessing the process. Viewers want the excitement and hard work that go into breaking a huge story. Aaron Sorkin’s latest film
The Social Reckoning
,
which dramatizes the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leaks, leaves viewers wanting more in this regard: more nosing around for sources, more poring over documents, more assembling the disparate pieces into a coherent whole.
Those familiar with Sorkin’s work know he is drawn to courtroom and courtroom-adjacent settings. These spaces grant Sorkin institutional gravitas and a real flesh-and-blood audience in the form of lawyers, judges, or other participants. Even Emily Mortimer’s MacKenzie McHale on
The Newsroom,
Sorkin’s TV drama about a fictional broadcast news network, pronounced, “That studio is a courtroom. And we only call expert witnesses.” Audiences may have forgotten (myself included) that Sorkin and David Fincher’s millennial masterpiece
The Social Network
,
a “companion piece” to
The Social Reckoning
, is narratively built around a pair of depositions. In those deposition scenes, Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg stares daggers at Andrew Garfield’s Eduardo Saverin and Armie Hammer’s Winklevoss twins while making pithy remarks about his own intellectual superiority. In Sorkin’s
Molly’s Game
, one key scene is a
criminal arraignment
. In
The Trial of the Chicago 7
, Sokin goes
full legal drama
. In
The Social Reckoning
, Sorkin gives viewers the courtroom with a twist: a Senate subcommittee hearing. If all the world’s a stage, the Capitol Building has the best acoustics for Sorkin to hear his own voice.
The film toggles back and forth between
Wall Street Journal
reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by a lackluster Jeremy Allen White, investigating the
“Facebook Files”
series in 2019 and 2020 and Zuckerberg’s rehearsal for his congressional testimony in 2021 (Sorkin
changed some
of the timeline details when adapting the true story for the silver screen). The film
finishes with former Facebook data scientist and Horwitz’s key source, Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, testifying before a congressional subcommittee. With this bifurcated structure,
The Social Reckoning
smashes two types of movies together. The effect is a courtroom-esque Sorkian drama dressed in the drag of a journalism movie. The film sprinkles in the key signifiers of the journalism movie, like covert source meetups and smoking-gun documents on a USB drive, in an attempt to signal its debt to classics by Alan J. Pakula or David Fincher, but these gestures feel hollow. Rather than effectively building the tension and drama around crafting a major story, Sorkin is more interested in carving out moment after moment for a character to spoon-feed the audience platitudes and convey the intricacies of Facebook’s manipulation of its own algorithm.
The Social Reckoning
is riddled with a strange lack of specificity. At no point do we see protagonist Jeff Horwitz sit down and write. White’s Horwitz spends as much time talking down to the women around him as he does investigating how Facebook’s reworked algorithm juices angrier, more polarizing content. His condescension had me cheering when Madison’s spitfire Frances Haugen repeatedly called him stupid. Horwitz frequently kicks his own work to student interns who take his calls late at night, but we don’t witness the work they have to do (create a fake account, go through documents, etc.). Much of the film revolves around Horwitz’s relationship with Haugen and the clandestine meetings where they discuss Facebook. But the film leans so heavily on his source building with her that the other components of breaking the story feel shortchanged by comparison.
Sorkin misunderstands the appeal of journalism films like
All the President’s Men,
where the tedium of journalism is a key part of the film’s drama. In one of the movie’s
most
iconic scenes
, Woodward and Bernstein sit in the Library of Congress and pore over documents. The camera, which is trained on the reporters from above, slowly pulls back, and they become two anonymous people sitting in the library.
Much like the other spaces he has occupied (the White House, the poker table), Sorkin uses the world of journalism as a stage where the heroes prevail. Even when things go wrong (such as when Jeff Daniels’s Will McAvoy in
The Newsroom
eats multiple weed cookies and has to go on the air) they are eventually righted in the end with Aristotelian panache (McAvoy reports the death of Osama bin Laden as if he were sober). Complex human relationships take a back seat to getting the job done right.
France Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) in Columbia Pictures' THE SOCIAL RECKONING. Courtesy of Sony Pictures
If Haugen and Horwitz are the heroes of the film, it’s obvious who Sorkin considers the bad guys. Facebook’s gradual but persistent colonization of people’s news-reading habits is portrayed like a virus, something that seems to have almost sprung up from nowhere but, before long, has taken hold of swaths of the population. The film begins with a red-pilled former leftist who posts an angry, racist tirade on Facebook. The woman turns out to be a former friend of Haugen’s. The movie includes a dramatization of the storming of the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, and the radicalized former leftist is among the insurrectionists. There are also references to Facebook as a dubious source of information, such as when a finance bro with whom Haugen goes on a date claims chlorophyll is a “natural internal deodorant," a tidbit he got from the social media platform.
Sorkin is also careful to convey to viewers that he does not think the work of journalists can be outsourced to social media companies. In one scene, Haugen snarls at Horwitz about how he simply resents that Facebook and social media are taking everyone’s jobs, and he retorts that that isn’t true. He just resents that they’re doing a shitty job of it.
But despite the heavy-handed outlook of
The Social Reckoning
, Sorkin doesn’t effectively convey the strength and power of truth-seeking journalism in filmic terms. The basic sentiment is present, as well as a general atmosphere of the decline of the press’ practical presence in people’s lives, but the overall effect is strangely hazy. Because the film does not commit to showing the less glamorous parts of reporting, all the supposed belief in journalism’s virtues ring hollow. It’s more of a source movie than a reporter one.
In the best journalism movies, the labor involved is dramatized, made to look, if not backbreaking, then at least mind-melting, exhausting. The indomitable stamina of the writers, the tedium of the method, is there to build tension, to give the act of storytelling its own mythology. In
The Social Reckoning
, Sorkin only offers Facebook status-ready flatness.
ICYMI: Interview with Mary Houlihan
On the latest podcast
episode
, Mary Houlihan, a comedian, discussed her humorous approach to independent reporting. In addition, she talked about her reporting on detention centers.
The episode is available on
Apple Podcasts
.
Can Journalism Be Funny? ft. Mary Houlihan
Podcast Episode · The Study Hall Podcast · October 19 · 33m
